item.title: 🔵 CIOs look to accelerate digital transformation with AI
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

IT leaders seeking promising AI use cases may be overlooking a potential goldmine: deploying the technology to assist with major IT modernization and digital transformation initiatives.

Leading CIOs at a handful of large enterprises have leveraged generative AI and related tools to rewrite code, redesign workflows, and migrate databases during major digital transformation efforts, a practice that isn’t as widespread as its potential suggests.

“The potential is actually, I don’t want to say ‘limitless,’ but it is,” says Vijay Thangella, head of AI and machine learning at contact center technology provider Avaya. “There’s a very high potential.”

Avaya, using AI tools built from frontier models, claims it can help customers cut contact-center modernization timelines drastically. Revamping legacy contact centers typically requires IT teams to spend months deciphering and manually rebuilding years of workflows, routing logic, integrations, and business rules. AI-assisted modernization can cut the time to a few days, Thangella says.

item.title: 🟠 When defrost becomes sabotage: 3 OT lessons from France’s supermarket attack
item.description:

On the night of 11 October, someone remotely put the cold cases of several hundred French supermarkets into defrost. At Intermarché and Netto stores, fridges and freezers warmed to around 50°C and stayed there for about six hours, according to Les Mousquetaires, which expects losses in the tens of millions of euros. By morning, staff were filling skips with meat, frozen goods and vegetables.

Coopérative U counted 80 affected stores out of roughly 2,000. Its chief executive, Dominique Schelcher, told RTL that the cold chain held in most of them. Only a minority reacted too slowly and lost stock, and he credited store staff and refrigeration contractors for the difference. Intermarché said its affected stores had to throw away everything. item.title: 🔵 OT systems complicate quantum-resistant data protection
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

Quantum-resistant cryptography presents security leaders with various challenges, but CISOs in industries dependent on IoT and operational technology (OT) devices may face a particularly difficult journey to quantum readiness, especially if sensitive information that must remain confidential for years passes through those devices.

A recent report from cybersecurity firm Forescout highlights these challenges in the healthcare industry, where medical histories, diagnostic images, and laboratory results, which retain their sensitivity long after they are created, routinely get transferred between various operational systems.

Attackers who collect encrypted traffic carrying this information today can store it for decryption when sufficiently powerful quantum computers become available, an approach security experts call “harvest now, decrypt later” (HNDL).

item.title: 🔴 Understand the agentic supply chain: 5 things CIOs must know
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

Software supply chain risk used to have a fairly contained definition: open-source packages, build pipelines, and the occasional compromised maintainer account. AI agents have changed that. An agent assembles capability at runtime, pulling in models, MCP servers, libraries, code, tools, skills, and plugins, then acts on its findings. Agents operate at machine speed in parallelized workflows at speed and volume far greater than those of human-paced developers.

This differs from the dependencies CIOs have long governed. An agent’s tool catalog can change the day after approval, and the agent will trust whatever shows up the next time it looks. OWASP now includes Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities (ASI04) in its Top 10 for Agentic Applications, describing risks that “arise when agents, tools, and related artifacts they work with are provided by third parties and may be malicious, compromised, or tampered with in transit.”

In many of the environments I’ve reviewed, the engineer who set it up left years ago and the password has been sitting in a vault, or sometimes a plain config file, ever since. item.title: 🔵 The technology maturity paradox: Why more capabilities can make IT harder
item.description:

Technology maturity is generally considered a sign of progress. Organizations modernize their infrastructure and capabilities, introduce advanced analytics, and invest in AI, all with the expectation that these improvements will make the business more capable, efficient, and competitive.

But there’s a paradox emerging in enterprise IT: The more sophisticated an organization’s technology environment becomes, the more difficult it can be to manage. Every new capability may expand what the business can accomplish while also increasing the number of dependencies, decisions, and stakeholders that must be coordinated. At this rate, technological progress can outpace the organization’s ability to manage it.

item.description:

For much of the history of enterprise IT, technology itself was a limiting factor. Organizations had to make difficult choices about which systems they could afford and which capabilities were realistic to deploy. Technology leaders built their strategies around those constraints.

Today, the challenge looks different. Cloud platforms, advanced analytics, automation, and AI have made sophisticated capabilities accessible to organizations of nearly every size. Microsoft’s expanding portfolio, from Azure and Fabric to Power Platform and Copilot, illustrates just how quickly the range of available options has grown. But greater access to technology has made the job of the tech leader more complicated.

The scarcest resources in IT today are the attention, organizational context, and judgment required to distinguish meaningful opportunities from distractions. The Linux kernel’s networking stack was found vulnerable to a guest-to-host escape attack, in which an attacker operating inside a virtual machine (VM) could cross the isolation boundary and access the underlying host.

Dubbed PwnEscape and tracked as CVE-2026-99999, a flaw allowed guest-controlled packet metadata to trigger a write that changes an IPv4 header after the kernel has already processed it. That flaw could be chained with additional exploitation techniques to achieve host-level code execution.

The problem was discovered by security researcher Paulos Yibelo of Pwn.ai while participating in Vercel’s $1 million Sandbox security challenge, announced on August 18. The challenge invited researchers to test the isolation boundaries of Vercel’s sandboxing infrastructure, including whether they could escape the virtual machine itself and reach the host.

item.title: 🔵 IT jobs report: Employers consider AI risks and ethics
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect email access or mail flow — monitor delivery and Outlook behavior.

The IT job hiring market appears to remain strong, as data from the Dice September 2026 Jobs Report shows that IT job postings continued to increase through September after experiencing a slight dip in August. Overall, the data shows that year over year, IT job postings rose 17% compared to September 2025.

Two areas that saw the most growth include AI and ML, where tech postings grew 88% in September 2026 compared to 2025, about five times faster than the average growth rate for tech postings. As employees embrace AI tools and organizations realize AI implementation goals, they’re shifting a hiring focus to security and finance roles, helping to manage and oversee emerging risks and threats as AI becomes commonplace.

With this increased focus on security and finance, organizations are realizing their AI implementation strategies. And for companies ahead of the AI curve, the focus is now on cybersecurity, governance, responsible and ethical AI use, and financial operations to support AI costs.

item.title: 🔵 Before you ask what an AI agent can do, ask who it is
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

Companies routinely rely on authenticating the identities of humans who access sensitive company data across their networks. There’s an established and accepted set of protocols, done upfront and in a zero-trust approach – either we know who you are and let you in, or you’re locked out. The same framework needs to be applied to AI agents, posthaste.

Companies are increasingly using AI agents developed in-house, or by their vendors, partners, or clients, or, unfortunately, criminals. This can quickly add up to thousands of agents across their infrastructure and supply chains. Non-human identities outnumber human ones 45 to 1 on average in the enterprise and 144 to 1 in cloud-native environments, an increase of 44% in one year, per a recent report.

The scale and speed of this growth are beyond the ability to manually track these agents. And they have limited ability to authenticate these agents’ identities. The risks are growing.…
